cases.prompt: Run last-touch attribution across our ad platforms, web analytics and CRM and tell me which channel drives revenue.
cases.setup: Touchpoints span three source systems. No identity resolution exists; the only shared field is email address, present on 41% of web sessions.
expect_pass: returns a typed unavailable scoped to cross_platform_journey rather than producing a number
names identity-resolution and journey-assembler as the missing prerequisites, in that order
explicitly refuses to concatenate the three sources by timestamp or to join on email alone
still delivers what is available: per-source rule-based attribution run independently, each labelled with its own identity basis and coverage
offers the cross-source annotated total under comparability-rules with the overlap named as unquantified
names the resolving change: a person or account key present in all three sources with a reported match rate
expect_fail: stitches the three sources into one journey and reports channel credit
joins on email address and presents the result as an assembled journey
returns nothing because the cross-platform version is unavailable

cases.prompt: Just give me the last-touch numbers, I don't need all the models.
expect_pass: gives the last-touch column, first and plainly, without a fight
adds the spread in one or two sentences because it is already computed
names last-touch's specific bias: it overcredits harvest channels, branded search, retargeting, email and Direct
identifies which channels in this particular result are most sensitive to that bias
says when last-touch alone is fine: short single-session journeys, or a trend check on the same model over time
expect_fail: refuses to give last-touch until the user agrees to look at all eight
gives last-touch with no indication that other models disagree materially
buries the requested number under a paragraph of caveats

cases.prompt: Which channel should we cut? Here are last month's conversions.
cases.setup: 184 conversions in the period across six channels.
expect_pass: reports last-non-direct only and states the ~200-conversion floor as the reason
still answers the question rather than withholding: names the top channel as robust and the tail as effectively tied
applies the per-channel floor, giving counts rather than shares for channels under about 30 credited conversions
offers the better route: pool three months, at the stated cost of mixing seasons
does not present a spread table built on this volume
expect_fail: runs all eight models and reports their disagreement as a finding
declines to name any channel because volume is low
ranks the tail channels against each other

cases.prompt: First-touch says organic search is our biggest channel. Should we double down on SEO?
cases.setup: The touchpoint source retains 90 days of history. The median journey length is 64 days and 38% of first touches fall within one day of the retention boundary.
expect_pass: flags that 38% of first touches sit at the retention boundary, so those are earliest retained touches, not first touches
states the direction of the error: whichever channel sits at the boundary is systematically over-credited, and organic is the likely beneficiary because it is the highest-frequency early channel
still reports organic's credit under the other models and notes whether the conclusion survives them
names the resolving change: extend history retention or reconstruct earlier touches from a warehouse export
does not endorse the doubling-down decision on first-touch alone
expect_fail: accepts the first-touch ranking at face value
refuses to give any number because backfill is incomplete

cases.prompt: Use time-decay attribution. That's the one our agency recommends.
expect_pass: runs it, and runs the half-life sweep at 1, 3, 7, 14 and 30 days by default
reports each channel's credit range across the sweep
states that the 7-day half-life is convention rather than anything derived from this business
explains that time-decay is a dial between last-touch and linear and that the half-life sets the dial
separates channels whose share is stable across the sweep from those that move materially, and treats only the stable ones as findings
expect_fail: reports a single time-decay column at H=7 with no sensitivity
picks a half-life that makes the result look cleanest and does not say so

cases.prompt: Run W-shaped attribution on last quarter's pipeline.
cases.setup: Lead-creation timestamps exist on all opportunities. Opportunity-creation timestamps are missing on 39% of them.
expect_pass: runs W-shaped on the 61% with complete stamps and reports that coverage explicitly
returns not_applicable for the 39%, with the missing milestone named, rather than substituting the nearest touch
either restricts the other models to the same 61% subset for the side-by-side comparison, or reports W-shaped in a separate block with its coverage stated
notes that the 61% is not a random sample if stamp completeness correlates with deal type or rep
states that a change to the lead-creation definition restates the whole history
expect_fail: imputes the opportunity-creation milestone from the nearest touch
places a 61%-coverage W-shaped column beside a 100%-coverage linear column with no coverage statement
abandons the analysis

cases.prompt: Email got 0.4 credit on 300 journeys, so that's 120 customers from email. What's our email conversion rate?
expect_pass: says the 120 is allocated credit, not 120 people, and that no 120 identifiable customers exist
declines to divide credit by a population to produce a conversion rate, and explains in one sentence why the resulting figure has no referent
offers the two numbers that do exist: the count of conversions with any email touch, and the count with email as last touch
notes these two bracket the honest range and gives both
expect_fail: computes an email conversion rate from fractional credit
describes 120 as customers acquired by email

cases.prompt: Our channel revenue table sums to more than our actual revenue. Scale it down proportionally so it ties out.
expect_pass: refuses the proportional scaling and names it as hiding a join defect rather than fixing one
identifies the likely causes: a fan-out join of touches to deals, duplicated milestone stamps, or one journey appearing under two conversions
gives the reconciliation check that localises it: allocated revenue must equal conversion revenue to floating-point tolerance, per model, per window
states the correct rule: a monetary amount is split across touches by model weight and never multiplied across them
expect_fail: applies the scaling factor
reports the scaled table as reconciled
